When the consequence is arbitrary code execution, this can often be used to subvert any other security service.

1220.name: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
1220.summary: The product implements access controls via a policy or other feature with the intention to disable or restrict accesses (reads and/or writes) to assets in a system from untrusted agents. However, implemented access controls lack required granularity, which renders the control policy too broad because it allows accesses from unauthorized agents to the security-sensitive assets.

1221.name: Incorrect Register Defaults or Module Parameters
1221.summary: Hardware description language code incorrectly defines register defaults or hardware Intellectual Property (IP) parameters to insecure values.

consequences.note: Degradation of system functionality, or loss of access control enforcement can occur.

1222.name: Insufficient Granularity of Address Regions Protected by Register Locks
1222.summary: The product defines a large address region protected from modification by the same register lock control bit. This results in a conflict between the functional requirement that some addresses need to be writable by software during operation and the security requirement that the system configuration lock bit must be set during the boot process.

consequences.note: System security configuration cannot be defined in a way that does not conflict with functional requirements of device.

1223.name: Race Condition for Write-Once Attributes
1223.summary: A write-once register in hardware design is programmable by an untrusted software component earlier than the trusted software component, resulting in a race condition issue.

consequences.note: System configuration cannot be programmed in a secure way.

1224.name: Improper Restriction of Write-Once Bit Fields
1224.summary: The hardware design control register "sticky bits" or write-once bit fields are improperly implemented, such that they can be reprogrammed by software.

consequences.note: System configuration cannot be programmed in a secure way.

1229.name: Creation of Emergent Resource
1229.summary: The product manages resources or behaves in a way that indirectly creates a new, distinct resource that can be used by attackers in violation of the intended policy.

123.name: Write-what-where Condition
123.summary: Any condition where the attacker has the ability to write an arbitrary value to an arbitrary location, often as the result of a buffer overflow.

consequences.note: Clearly, write-what-where conditions can be used to write data to areas of memory outside the scope of a policy. Also, they almost invariably can be used to execute arbitrary code, which is usually outside the scope of a
Many memory accesses can lead to program termination, such as when writing to addresses that are invalid for the current process.
When the consequence is arbitrary code execution, this can often be used to subvert any other security service.

1230.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information Through Metadata
1230.summary: The product prevents direct access to a resource containing sensitive information, but it does not sufficiently limit access to metadata that is derived from the original, sensitive information.

1231.name: Improper Prevention of Lock Bit Modification
1231.summary: The product uses a trusted lock bit for restricting access to registers, address regions, or other resources, but the product does not prevent the value of the lock bit from being modified after it has been set.

consequences.note: Registers protected by lock bit can be modified even when lock is set.

1232.name: Improper Lock Behavior After Power State Transition
1232.summary: Register lock bit protection disables changes to system configuration once the bit is set. Some of the protected registers or lock bits become programmable after power state transitions (e.g., Entry and wake from low power sleep modes) causing the system configuration to be changeable.

1233.name: Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
1233.summary: The product uses a register lock bit protection mechanism, but it does not ensure that the lock bit prevents modification of system registers or controls that perform changes to important hardware system configuration.

consequences.note: System Configuration protected by the lock bit can be modified even when the lock is set.

1234.name: Hardware Internal or Debug Modes Allow Override of Locks
1234.summary: System configuration protection may be bypassed during debug mode.

consequences.note: Bypass of lock bit allows access and modification of system configuration even when the lock bit is set.

1235.name: Incorrect Use of Autoboxing and Unboxing for Performance Critical Operations
1235.summary: The code uses boxed primitives, which may introduce inefficiencies into performance-critical operations.

consequences.note: Incorrect autoboxing/unboxing would result in reduced performance, which sometimes can lead to resource consumption issues.

1236.name: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File
1236.summary: The product saves user-provided information into a Comma-Separated Value (CSV) file, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as a command when the file is opened by a spreadsheet product.

consequences.note: Current versions of Excel warn users of untrusted content.

1239.name: Improper Zeroization of Hardware Register
1239.summary: The hardware product does not properly clear sensitive information from built-in registers when the user of the hardware block changes.

consequences.note: The consequences will depend on the information disclosed due to the vulnerability.

124.name: Buffer Underwrite ('Buffer Underflow')
124.summary: The product writes to a buffer using an index or pointer that references a memory location prior to the beginning of the buffer.

consequences.note: Out of bounds memory access will very likely result in the corruption of relevant memory, and perhaps instructions, possibly leading to a crash.

If the corrupted memory can be effectively controlled, it may be possible to execute arbitrary code. If the corrupted memory is data rather than instructions, the system will continue to function with improper changes, p
When the consequence is arbitrary code execution, this can often be used to subvert any other security service.

1240.name: Use of a Cryptographic Primitive with a Risky Implementation
1240.summary: To fulfill the need for a cryptographic primitive, the product implements a cryptographic algorithm using a non-standard, unproven, or disallowed/non-compliant cryptographic implementation.

consequences.note: Incorrect usage of crypto primitives could render the supposedly encrypted data as unencrypted plaintext in the worst case.

1241.name: Use of Predictable Algorithm in Random Number Generator
1241.summary: The device uses an algorithm that is predictable and generates a pseudo-random number.

1242.name: Inclusion of Undocumented Features or Chicken Bits
1242.summary: The device includes chicken bits or undocumented features that can create entry points for unauthorized actors.

1243.name: Sensitive Non-Volatile Information Not Protected During Debug
1243.summary: Access to security-sensitive information stored in fuses is not limited during debug.

1244.name: Internal Asset Exposed to Unsafe Debug Access Level or State
1244.summary: The product uses physical debug or test interfaces with support for multiple access levels, but it assigns the wrong debug access level to an internal asset, providing unintended access to the asset from untrusted debug agents.

1245.name: Improper Finite State Machines (FSMs) in Hardware Logic
1245.summary: Faulty finite state machines (FSMs) in the hardware logic allow an attacker to put the system in an undefined state, to cause a denial of service (DoS) or gain privileges on the victim's system.

1246.name: Improper Write Handling in Limited-write Non-Volatile Memories
1246.summary: The product does not implement or incorrectly implements wear leveling operations in limited-write non-volatile memories.

1247.name: Improper Protection Against Voltage and Clock Glitches
1247.summary: The device does not contain or contains incorrectly implemented circuitry or sensors to detect and mitigate voltage and clock glitches and protect sensitive information or software contained on the device.

1248.name: Semiconductor Defects in Hardware Logic with Security-Sensitive Implications
1248.summary: The security-sensitive hardware module contains semiconductor defects.

1249.name: Application-Level Admin Tool with Inconsistent View of Underlying Operating System
1249.summary: The product provides an application for administrators to manage parts of the underlying operating system, but the application does not accurately identify all of the relevant entities or resources that exist in the OS; that is, the application's model of the OS's state is inconsistent with the OS's actual state.

125.name: Out-of-bounds Read
125.summary: The product reads data past the end, or before the beginning, of the intended buffer.

consequences.note: An attacker could get secret values such as cryptographic keys, PII, memory addresses, or other information that could be used in additional attacks.

Out-of-bounds memory could contain memory addresses or other information that can be used to bypass ASLR and other protection mechanisms in order to improve the reliability of exploiting a separate weakness for code exec

An attacker could cause a segmentation fault or crash by causing memory to be read outside of the bounds of the buffer. This is especially likely when the code reads a variable amount of data and assumes that a sentinel
The read operation could produce other undefined or unexpected results.

1250.name: Improper Preservation of Consistency Between Independent Representations of Shared State
1250.summary: The product has or supports multiple distributed components or sub-systems that are each required to keep their own local copy of shared data - such as state or cache - but the product does not ensure that all local copies remain consistent with each other.

1251.name: Mirrored Regions with Different Values
1251.summary: The product's architecture mirrors regions without ensuring that their contents always stay in sync.

1252.name: CPU Hardware Not Configured to Support Exclusivity of Write and Execute Operations
1252.summary: The CPU is not configured to provide hardware support for exclusivity of write and execute operations on memory. This allows an attacker to execute data from all of memory.

1253.name: Incorrect Selection of Fuse Values
1253.summary: The logic level used to set a system to a secure state relies on a fuse being unblown. An attacker can set the system to an insecure state merely by blowing the fuse.

1254.name: Incorrect Comparison Logic Granularity
1254.summary: The product's comparison logic is performed over a series of steps rather than across the entire string in one operation. If there is a comparison logic failure on one of these steps, the operation may be vulnerable to a timing attack that can result in the interception of the process for nefarious purposes.

1255.name: Comparison Logic is Vulnerable to Power Side-Channel Attacks
1255.summary: A device's real time power consumption may be monitored during security token evaluation and the information gleaned may be used to determine the value of the reference token.

consequences.note: As compromising a security token may result in complete system control, the impacts are relatively universal.

1256.name: Improper Restriction of Software Interfaces to Hardware Features
1256.summary: The product provides software-controllable device functionality for capabilities such as power and clock management, but it does not properly limit functionality that can lead to modification of hardware memory or register bits, or the ability to observe physical side channels.

1257.name: Improper Access Control Applied to Mirrored or Aliased Memory Regions
1257.summary: Aliased or mirrored memory regions in hardware designs may have inconsistent read/write permissions enforced by the hardware. A possible result is that an untrusted agent is blocked from accessing a memory region but is not blocked from accessing the corresponding aliased memory region.

1258.name: Exposure of Sensitive System Information Due to Uncleared Debug Information
1258.summary: The hardware does not fully clear security-sensitive values, such as keys and intermediate values in cryptographic operations, when debug mode is entered.

1259.name: Improper Restriction of Security Token Assignment
1259.summary: The System-On-A-Chip (SoC) implements a Security Token mechanism to differentiate what actions are allowed or disallowed when a transaction originates from an entity. However, the Security Tokens are improperly protected.

126.name: Buffer Over-read
126.summary: The product reads from a buffer using buffer access mechanisms such as indexes or pointers that reference memory locations after the targeted buffer.

consequences.note: By reading out-of-bounds memory, an attacker might be able to get secret values, such as memory addresses, which can be bypass protection mechanisms such as ASLR in order to improve the reliability and likelihood of expl

1260.name: Improper Handling of Overlap Between Protected Memory Ranges
1260.summary: The product allows address regions to overlap, which can result in the bypassing of intended memory protection.

1261.name: Improper Handling of Single Event Upsets
1261.summary: The hardware logic does not effectively handle when single-event upsets (SEUs) occur.

1262.name: Improper Access Control for Register Interface
1262.summary: The product uses memory-mapped I/O registers that act as an interface to hardware functionality from software, but there is improper access control to those registers.

consequences.note: Confidentiality of hardware assets may be violated if the protected information can be read out by software through the register interface. Registers storing security state, settings, other security-critical data may be

1263.name: Improper Physical Access Control
1263.summary: The product is designed with access restricted to certain information, but it does not sufficiently protect against an unauthorized actor with physical access to these areas.

1264.name: Hardware Logic with Insecure De-Synchronization between Control and Data Channels
1264.summary: The hardware logic for error handling and security checks can incorrectly forward data before the security check is complete.

1265.name: Unintended Reentrant Invocation of Non-reentrant Code Via Nested Calls
1265.summary: During execution of non-reentrant code, the product performs a call that unintentionally produces a nested invocation of the non-reentrant code.

consequences.note: Exploitation of this weakness can leave the application in an unexpected state and cause variables to be reassigned before the first invocation has completed. This may eventually result in memory corruption or unexpected

1266.name: Improper Scrubbing of Sensitive Data from Decommissioned Device
1266.summary: The product does not properly provide a capability for the product administrator to remove sensitive data at the time the product is decommissioned. A scrubbing capability could be missing, insufficient, or incorrect.

1267.name: Policy Uses Obsolete Encoding
1267.summary: The product uses an obsolete encoding mechanism to implement access controls.

1268.name: Policy Privileges are not Assigned Consistently Between Control and Data Agents
1268.summary: The product's hardware-enforced access control for a particular resource improperly accounts for privilege discrepancies between control and write policies.

1269.name: Product Released in Non-Release Configuration
1269.summary: The product released to market is released in pre-production or manufacturing configuration.

127.name: Buffer Under-read
127.summary: The product reads from a buffer using buffer access mechanisms such as indexes or pointers that reference memory locations prior to the targeted buffer.

consequences.note: By reading out-of-bounds memory, an attacker might be able to get secret values, such as memory addresses, which can be bypass protection mechanisms such as ASLR in order to improve the reliability and likelihood of expl

1270.name: Generation of Incorrect Security Tokens
1270.summary: The product implements a Security Token mechanism to differentiate what actions are allowed or disallowed when a transaction originates from an entity. However, the Security Tokens generated in the system are incorrect.

1271.name: Uninitialized Value on Reset for Registers Holding Security Settings
1271.summary: Security-critical logic is not set to a known value on reset.

1272.name: Sensitive Information Uncleared Before Debug/Power State Transition
1272.summary: The product performs a power or debug state transition, but it does not clear sensitive information that should no longer be accessible due to changes to information access restrictions.

consequences.note: Sensitive information may be used to unlock additional capabilities of the device and take advantage of hidden functionalities which could be used to compromise device security.

1273.name: Device Unlock Credential Sharing
1273.summary: The credentials necessary for unlocking a device are shared across multiple parties and may expose sensitive information.

consequences.note: Once unlock credentials are compromised, an attacker can use the credentials to unlock the device and gain unauthorized access to the hidden functionalities protected by those credentials.

1274.name: Improper Access Control for Volatile Memory Containing Boot Code
1274.summary: The product conducts a secure-boot process that transfers bootloader code from Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) into Volatile Memory (VM), but it does not have sufficient access control or other protections for the Volatile Memory.

1275.name: Sensitive Cookie with Improper SameSite Attribute
1275.summary: The SameSite attribute for sensitive cookies is not set, or an insecure value is used.

consequences.note: If the website does not impose additional defense against CSRF attacks, failing to use the 'Lax' or 'Strict' values could increase the risk of exposure to CSRF attacks. The likelihood of the integrity breach is Low becau

1276.name: Hardware Child Block Incorrectly Connected to Parent System
1276.summary: Signals between a hardware IP and the parent system design are incorrectly connected causing security risks.

1277.name: Firmware Not Updateable
1277.summary: The product does not provide its users with the ability to update or patch its firmware to address any vulnerabilities or weaknesses that may be present.

consequences.note: If an attacker can identify an exploitable vulnerability in one device that has no means of patching, the attack may be used against an entire class of devices.

1278.name: Missing Protection Against Hardware Reverse Engineering Using Integrated Circuit (IC) Imaging Techniques
1278.summary: Information stored in hardware may be recovered by an attacker with the capability to capture and analyze images of the integrated circuit using techniques such as scanning electron microscopy.

consequences.note: A common goal of malicious actors who reverse engineer ICs is to produce and sell counterfeit versions of the IC.

1279.name: Cryptographic Operations are run Before Supporting Units are Ready
1279.summary: Performing cryptographic operations without ensuring that the supporting inputs are ready to supply valid data may compromise the cryptographic result.

128.name: Wrap-around Error
128.summary: Wrap around errors occur whenever a value is incremented past the maximum value for its type and therefore "wraps around" to a very small, negative, or undefined value.

consequences.note: This weakness will generally lead to undefined behavior and therefore crashes. In the case of overflows involving loop index variables, the likelihood of infinite loops is also high.

If the value in question is important to data (as opposed to flow), simple data corruption has occurred. Also, if the wrap around results in other conditions such as buffer overflows, further memory corruption may occur.
This weakness can sometimes trigger buffer overflows which can be used to execute arbitrary code. This is usually outside the scope of a program's implicit security policy.

1280.name: Access Control Check Implemented After Asset is Accessed
1280.summary: A product's hardware-based access control check occurs after the asset has been accessed.

1281.name: Sequence of Processor Instructions Leads to Unexpected Behavior
1281.summary: Specific combinations of processor instructions lead to undesirable behavior such as locking the processor until a hard reset performed.

1282.name: Assumed-Immutable Data is Stored in Writable Memory
1282.summary: Immutable data, such as a first-stage bootloader, device identifiers, and "write-once" configuration settings are stored in writable memory that can be re-programmed or updated in the field.

1283.name: Mutable Attestation or Measurement Reporting Data
1283.summary: The register contents used for attestation or measurement reporting data to verify boot flow are modifiable by an adversary.

1284.name: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input
1284.summary: The product receives input that is expected to specify a quantity (such as size or length), but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the quantity has the required properties.

consequences.note: Since quantities are used so often to affect resource allocation or process financial data, they are often present in many places in the code.

1285.name: Improper Validation of Specified Index, Position, or Offset in Input
1285.summary: The product receives input that is expected to specify an index, position, or offset into an indexable resource such as a buffer or file, but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the specified index/position/offset has the required properties.

1286.name: Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input
1286.summary: The product receives input that is expected to be well-formed - i.e., to comply with a certain syntax - but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the input complies with the syntax.

1287.name: Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input
1287.summary: The product receives input that is expected to be of a certain type, but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the input is actually of the expected type.

1288.name: Improper Validation of Consistency within Input
1288.summary: The product receives a complex input with multiple elements or fields that must be consistent with each other, but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the input is actually consistent.

1289.name: Improper Validation of Unsafe Equivalence in Input
1289.summary: The product receives an input value that is used as a resource identifier or other type of reference, but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the input is equivalent to a potentially-unsafe value.

129.name: Improper Validation of Array Index
129.summary: The product uses untrusted input when calculating or using an array index, but the product does not validate or incorrectly validates the index to ensure the index references a valid position within the array.

consequences.note: Use of an index that is outside the bounds of an array will very likely result in the corruption of relevant memory and perhaps instructions, leading to a crash, if the values are outside of the valid memory area.
If the memory corrupted is data, rather than instructions, the system will continue to function with improper values.

Use of an index that is outside the bounds of an array can also trigger out-of-bounds read or write operations, or operations on the wrong objects; i.e., "buffer overflows" are not always the result. This may result in t

If the memory accessible by the attacker can be effectively controlled, it may be possible to execute arbitrary code, as with a standard buffer overflow and possibly without the use of large inputs if a precise index can

A single fault could allow either an overflow (CWE-788) or underflow (CWE-786) of the array index. What happens next will depend on the type of operation being performed out of bounds, but can expose sensitive informatio

1290.name: Incorrect Decoding of Security Identifiers
1290.summary: The product implements a decoding mechanism to decode certain bus-transaction signals to security identifiers. If the decoding is implemented incorrectly, then untrusted agents can now gain unauthorized access to the asset.

1291.name: Public Key Re-Use for Signing both Debug and Production Code
1291.summary: The same public key is used for signing both debug and production code.

1292.name: Incorrect Conversion of Security Identifiers
1292.summary: The product implements a conversion mechanism to map certain bus-transaction signals to security identifiers. However, if the conversion is incorrectly implemented, untrusted agents can gain unauthorized access to the asset.

1293.name: Missing Source Correlation of Multiple Independent Data
1293.summary: The product relies on one source of data, preventing the ability to detect if an adversary has compromised a data source.

consequences.note: An attacker that may be able to execute a single Person-in-the-Middle attack can subvert a check of an external oracle (e.g. the ACME protocol check for a file on a website), and thus inject an arbitrary reply to the sin

1294.name: Insecure Security Identifier Mechanism
1294.summary: The System-on-Chip (SoC) implements a Security Identifier mechanism to differentiate what actions are allowed or disallowed when a transaction originates from an entity. However, the Security Identifiers are not correctly implemented.

1295.name: Debug Messages Revealing Unnecessary Information
1295.summary: The product fails to adequately prevent the revealing of unnecessary and potentially sensitive system information within debugging messages.

1296.name: Incorrect Chaining or Granularity of Debug Components
1296.summary: The product's debug components contain incorrect chaining or granularity of debug components.

consequences.note: Depending on the access to debug component(s) erroneously granted, an attacker could use the debug component to gain additional understanding about the system to further an attack and/or execute other commands. This coul

1297.name: Unprotected Confidential Information on Device is Accessible by OSAT Vendors
1297.summary: The product does not adequately protect confidential information on the device from being accessed by Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) vendors.

consequences.note: The impact depends on the confidential information itself and who is inadvertently granted access. For example, if the confidential information is a key that can unlock all the parts of a generation, the impact could be

1298.name: Hardware Logic Contains Race Conditions
1298.summary: A race condition in the hardware logic results in undermining security guarantees of the system.

1299.name: Missing Protection Mechanism for Alternate Hardware Interface
1299.summary: The lack of protections on alternate paths to access control-protected assets (such as unprotected shadow registers and other external facing unguarded interfaces) allows an attacker to bypass existing protections to the asset that are only performed against the primary path.

13.name: ASP.NET Misconfiguration: Password in Configuration File
13.summary: Storing a plaintext password in a configuration file allows anyone who can read the file access to the password-protected resource making them an easy target for attackers.

130.name: Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency
130.summary: The product parses a formatted message or structure, but it does not handle or incorrectly handles a length field that is inconsistent with the actual length of the associated data.

1300.name: Improper Protection of Physical Side Channels
1300.summary: The device does not contain sufficient protection mechanisms to prevent physical side channels from exposing sensitive information due to patterns in physically observable phenomena such as variations in power consumption, electromagnetic emissions (EME), or acoustic emissions.

1301.name: Insufficient or Incomplete Data Removal within Hardware Component
1301.summary: The product's data removal process does not completely delete all data and potentially sensitive information within hardware components.

1302.name: Missing Source Identifier in Entity Transactions on a System-On-Chip (SOC)
1302.summary: The product implements a security identifier mechanism to differentiate what actions are allowed or disallowed when a transaction originates from an entity. A transaction is sent without a security identifier.

1303.name: Non-Transparent Sharing of Microarchitectural Resources
1303.summary: Hardware structures shared across execution contexts (e.g., caches and branch predictors) can violate the expected architecture isolation between contexts.

consequences.note: Microarchitectural side-channels have been used to leak specific information such as cryptographic keys, and Address Space Layout Randomization (ALSR) offsets as well as arbitrary memory.

1304.name: Improperly Preserved Integrity of Hardware Configuration State During a Power Save/Restore Operation
1304.summary: The product performs a power save/restore operation, but it does not ensure that the integrity of the configuration state is maintained and/or verified between the beginning and ending of the operation.

131.name: Incorrect Calculation of Buffer Size
131.summary: The product does not correctly calculate the size to be used when allocating a buffer, which could lead to a buffer overflow.

consequences.note: If the incorrect calculation is used in the context of memory allocation, then the software may create a buffer that is smaller or larger than expected. If the allocated buffer is smaller than expected, this could lead t

1310.name: Missing Ability to Patch ROM Code
1310.summary: Missing an ability to patch ROM code may leave a System or System-on-Chip (SoC) in a vulnerable state.

consequences.note: When the system is unable to be patched, it can be left in a vulnerable state.

1311.name: Improper Translation of Security Attributes by Fabric Bridge
1311.summary: The bridge incorrectly translates security attributes from either trusted to untrusted or from untrusted to trusted when converting from one fabric protocol to another.

1312.name: Missing Protection for Mirrored Regions in On-Chip Fabric Firewall
1312.summary: The firewall in an on-chip fabric protects the main addressed region, but it does not protect any mirrored memory or memory-mapped-IO (MMIO) regions.

1313.name: Hardware Allows Activation of Test or Debug Logic at Runtime
1313.summary: During runtime, the hardware allows for test or debug logic (feature) to be activated, which allows for changing the state of the hardware. This feature can alter the intended behavior of the system and allow for alteration and leakage of sensitive data by an adversary.

1314.name: Missing Write Protection for Parametric Data Values
1314.summary: The device does not write-protect the parametric data values for sensors that scale the sensor value, allowing untrusted software to manipulate the apparent result and potentially damage hardware or cause operational failure.

consequences.note: Sensor value manipulation, particularly thermal or power, may allow physical damage to occur or disabling of the device by a false fault shutdown causing a Denial-Of-Service.

1315.name: Improper Setting of Bus Controlling Capability in Fabric End-point
1315.summary: The bus controller enables bits in the fabric end-point to allow responder devices to control transactions on the fabric.

1316.name: Fabric-Address Map Allows Programming of Unwarranted Overlaps of Protected and Unprotected Ranges
1316.summary: The address map of the on-chip fabric has protected and unprotected regions overlapping, allowing an attacker to bypass access control to the overlapping portion of the protected region.

1317.name: Improper Access Control in Fabric Bridge
1317.summary: The product uses a fabric bridge for transactions between two Intellectual Property (IP) blocks, but the bridge does not properly perform the expected privilege, identity, or other access control checks between those IP blocks.

1318.name: Missing Support for Security Features in On-chip Fabrics or Buses
1318.summary: On-chip fabrics or buses either do not support or are not configured to support privilege separation or other security features, such as access control.

1319.name: Improper Protection against Electromagnetic Fault Injection (EM-FI)
1319.summary: The device is susceptible to electromagnetic fault injection attacks, causing device internal information to be compromised or security mechanisms to be bypassed.

132.name: DEPRECATED: Miscalculated Null Termination
132.summary: This entry has been deprecated because it was a duplicate of CWE-170. All content has been transferred to CWE-170.

1320.name: Improper Protection for Outbound Error Messages and Alert Signals
1320.summary: Untrusted agents can disable alerts about signal conditions exceeding limits or the response mechanism that handles such alerts.

1321.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution')
1321.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component that specifies attributes that are to be initialized or updated in an object, but it does not properly control modifications of attributes of the object prototype.

consequences.note: An attacker can inject attributes that are used in other components.
An attacker can override existing attributes with ones that have incompatible type, which may lead to a crash.

1322.name: Use of Blocking Code in Single-threaded, Non-blocking Context
1322.summary: The product uses a non-blocking model that relies on a single threaded process for features such as scalability, but it contains code that can block when it is invoked.

consequences.note: An unexpected call to blocking code can trigger an infinite loop, or a large loop that causes the software to pause and wait indefinitely.

1323.name: Improper Management of Sensitive Trace Data
1323.summary: Trace data collected from several sources on the System-on-Chip (SoC) is stored in unprotected locations or transported to untrusted agents.

consequences.note: An adversary can read secret values if they are captured in debug traces and stored unsafely.

1324.name: DEPRECATED: Sensitive Information Accessible by Physical Probing of JTAG Interface
1324.summary: This entry has been deprecated because it was at a lower level of abstraction than supported by CWE. All relevant content has been integrated into CWE-319.

1325.name: Improperly Controlled Sequential Memory Allocation
1325.summary: The product manages a group of objects or resources and performs a separate memory allocation for each object, but it does not properly limit the total amount of memory that is consumed by all of the combined objects.

consequences.note: Not controlling memory allocation can result in a request for too much system memory, possibly leading to a crash of the application due to out-of-memory conditions, or the consumption of a large amount of memory on the

1326.name: Missing Immutable Root of Trust in Hardware
1326.summary: A missing immutable root of trust in the hardware results in the ability to bypass secure boot or execute untrusted or adversarial boot code.

1327.name: Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address
1327.summary: The product assigns the address 0.0.0.0 for a database server, a cloud service/instance, or any computing resource that communicates remotely.

1328.name: Security Version Number Mutable to Older Versions
1328.summary: Security-version number in hardware is mutable, resulting in the ability to downgrade (roll-back) the boot firmware to vulnerable code versions.

consequences.note: Impact includes roll-back or downgrade to a vulnerable version of the firmware or DoS (prevent upgrades).

1329.name: Reliance on Component That is Not Updateable
1329.summary: The product contains a component that cannot be updated or patched in order to remove vulnerabilities or significant bugs.

consequences.note: If an attacker can identify an exploitable vulnerability in one product that has no means of patching, the attack may be used against all affected versions of that product.

1330.name: Remanent Data Readable after Memory Erase
1330.summary: Confidential information stored in memory circuits is readable or recoverable after being cleared or erased.

consequences.note: Confidential data are readable to untrusted agent.

1331.name: Improper Isolation of Shared Resources in Network On Chip (NoC)
1331.summary: The Network On Chip (NoC) does not isolate or incorrectly isolates its on-chip-fabric and internal resources such that they are shared between trusted and untrusted agents, creating timing channels.

consequences.note: Attackers may infer data that belongs to a trusted agent. The methods used to perform this attack may result in noticeably increased resource consumption.

1332.name: Improper Handling of Faults that Lead to Instruction Skips
1332.summary: The device is missing or incorrectly implements circuitry or sensors that detect and mitigate the skipping of security-critical CPU instructions when they occur.

consequences.note: Depending on the context, instruction skipping can have a broad range of consequences related to the generic bypassing of security critical code.

1333.name: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity
1333.summary: The product uses a regular expression with an inefficient, possibly exponential worst-case computational complexity that consumes excessive CPU cycles.

1334.name: Unauthorized Error Injection Can Degrade Hardware Redundancy
1334.summary: An unauthorized agent can inject errors into a redundant block to deprive the system of redundancy or put the system in a degraded operating mode.

1335.name: Incorrect Bitwise Shift of Integer
1335.summary: An integer value is specified to be shifted by a negative amount or an amount greater than or equal to the number of bits contained in the value causing an unexpected or indeterminate result.

1336.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine
1336.summary: The product uses a template engine to insert or process externally-influenced input, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements or syntax that can be interpreted as template expressions or other code directives when processed by the engine.

1338.name: Improper Protections Against Hardware Overheating
1338.summary: A hardware device is missing or has inadequate protection features to prevent overheating.

1339.name: Insufficient Precision or Accuracy of a Real Number
1339.summary: The product processes a real number with an implementation in which the number's representation does not preserve required accuracy and precision in its fractional part, causing an incorrect result.

consequences.note: This weakness will generally lead to undefined results and therefore crashes. In some implementations the program will halt if the weakness causes an overflow during a calculation.
The results of the math are not as expected. This could cause issues where a value would not be properly calculated and provide an incorrect answer.
This weakness can sometimes trigger buffer overflows which can be used to execute arbitrary code. This is usually outside the scope of a product's implicit security policy.

134.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Format String
134.summary: The product uses a function that accepts a format string as an argument, but the format string originates from an external source.

consequences.note: Format string problems allow for information disclosure which can severely simplify exploitation of the program.
Format string problems can result in the execution of arbitrary code.

1341.name: Multiple Releases of Same Resource or Handle
1341.summary: The product attempts to close or release a resource or handle more than once, without any successful open between the close operations.

1342.name: Information Exposure through Microarchitectural State after Transient Execution
1342.summary: The processor does not properly clear microarchitectural state after incorrect microcode assists or speculative execution, resulting in transient execution.

135.name: Incorrect Calculation of Multi-Byte String Length
135.summary: The product does not correctly calculate the length of strings that can contain wide or multi-byte characters.

consequences.note: This weakness may lead to a buffer overflow. Buffer overflows often can be used to execute arbitrary code, which is usually outside the scope of a program's implicit security policy. This can often be used to subvert any

1351.name: Improper Handling of Hardware Behavior in Exceptionally Cold Environments
1351.summary: A hardware device, or the firmware running on it, is missing or has incorrect protection features to maintain goals of security primitives when the device is cooled below standard operating temperatures.

consequences.note: Consequences of this weakness are highly contextual.

1357.name: Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component
1357.summary: The product is built from multiple separate components, but it uses a component that is not sufficiently trusted to meet expectations for security, reliability, updateability, and maintainability.

138.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements
138.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as control elements or syntactic markers when they are sent to a downstream component.

1384.name: Improper Handling of Physical or Environmental Conditions
1384.summary: The product does not properly handle unexpected physical or environmental conditions that occur naturally or are artificially induced.

consequences.note: Consequences of this weakness are highly dependent on the role of affected components within the larger product.

1385.name: Missing Origin Validation in WebSockets
1385.summary: The product uses a WebSocket, but it does not properly verify that the source of data or communication is valid.

consequences.note: The consequences will vary depending on the nature of the functionality that is vulnerable to CSRF. An attacker could effectively perform any operations as the victim. If the victim is an administrator or privileged user

1386.name: Insecure Operation on Windows Junction / Mount Point
1386.summary: The product opens a file or directory, but it does not properly prevent the name from being associated with a junction or mount point to a destination that is outside of the intended control sphere.

consequences.note: Read arbitrary files by replacing a user-controlled folder with a mount point and additional hard links.
Modify an arbitrary file by replacing the rollback files in installer directories, as they can have the installer execute those rollbacks.

1389.name: Incorrect Parsing of Numbers with Different Radices
1389.summary: The product parses numeric input assuming base 10 (decimal) values, but it does not account for inputs that use a different base number (radix).

consequences.note: An attacker may use an unexpected numerical base to access private application resources.
An attacker may use an unexpected numerical base to bypass or manipulate access control mechanisms.

1390.name: Weak Authentication
1390.summary: The product uses an authentication mechanism to restrict access to specific users or identities, but the mechanism does not sufficiently prove that the claimed identity is correct.

consequences.note: This weakness can lead to the exposure of resources or functionality to unintended actors, possibly providing attackers with sensitive information or even execute arbitrary code.

1391.name: Use of Weak Credentials
1391.summary: The product uses weak credentials (such as a default key or hard-coded password) that can be calculated, derived, reused, or guessed by an attacker.

1392.name: Use of Default Credentials
1392.summary: The product uses default credentials (such as passwords or cryptographic keys) for potentially critical functionality.

1393.name: Use of Default Password
1393.summary: The product uses default passwords for potentially critical functionality.

1394.name: Use of Default Cryptographic Key
1394.summary: The product uses a default cryptographic key for potentially critical functionality.

1395.name: Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component
1395.summary: The product has a dependency on a third-party component that contains one or more known vulnerabilities.

consequences.note: The consequences vary widely, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in the component; how those vulnerabilities can be "reached" by adversaries, as the exploitation paths and attack surface will vary depending on h

14.name: Compiler Removal of Code to Clear Buffers
14.summary: Sensitive memory is cleared according to the source code, but compiler optimizations leave the memory untouched when it is not read from again, aka "dead store removal."

consequences.note: This weakness will allow data that has not been cleared from memory to be read. If this data contains sensitive password information, then an attacker can read the password and use the information to bypass protection me

140.name: Improper Neutralization of Delimiters
140.summary: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes delimiters.

141.name: Improper Neutralization of Parameter/Argument Delimiters
141.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as parameter or argument delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

1419.name: Incorrect Initialization of Resource
1419.summary: The product attempts to initialize a resource but does not correctly do so, which might leave the resource in an unexpected, incorrect, or insecure state when it is accessed.

consequences.note: The technical impact can vary widely based on how the resource is used in the product, and whether its contents affect security decisions.

142.name: Improper Neutralization of Value Delimiters
142.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as value delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

1420.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information during Transient Execution
1420.summary: A processor event or prediction may allow incorrect operations (or correct operations with incorrect data) to execute transiently, potentially exposing data over a covert channel.

1421.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information in Shared Microarchitectural Structures during Transient Execution
1421.summary: A processor event may allow transient operations to access architecturally restricted data (for example, in another address space) in a shared microarchitectural structure (for example, a CPU cache), potentially exposing the data over a covert channel.

consequences.note: <<put the information here>>

1422.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information caused by Incorrect Data Forwarding during Transient Execution
1422.summary: A processor event or prediction may allow incorrect or stale data to be forwarded to transient operations, potentially exposing data over a covert channel.

1423.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information caused by Shared Microarchitectural Predictor State that Influences Transient Execution
1423.summary: Shared microarchitectural predictor state may allow code to influence transient execution across a hardware boundary, potentially exposing data that is accessible beyond the boundary over a covert channel.

1426.name: Improper Validation of Generative AI Output
1426.summary: The product invokes a generative AI/ML component whose behaviors and outputs cannot be directly controlled, but the product does not validate or insufficiently validates the outputs to ensure that they align with the intended security, content, or privacy policy.

143.name: Improper Neutralization of Record Delimiters
143.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as record delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

144.name: Improper Neutralization of Line Delimiters
144.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as line delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

145.name: Improper Neutralization of Section Delimiters
145.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as section delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

146.name: Improper Neutralization of Expression/Command Delimiters
146.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as expression or command delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

147.name: Improper Neutralization of Input Terminators
147.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as input terminators when they are sent to a downstream component.

148.name: Improper Neutralization of Input Leaders
148.summary: The product does not properly handle when a leading character or sequence ("leader") is missing or malformed, or if multiple leaders are used when only one should be allowed.

149.name: Improper Neutralization of Quoting Syntax
149.summary: Quotes injected into a product can be used to compromise a system. As data are parsed, an injected/absent/duplicate/malformed use of quotes may cause the process to take unexpected actions.

15.name: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
15.summary: One or more system settings or configuration elements can be externally controlled by a user.

150.name: Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences
150.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as escape, meta, or control character sequences when they are sent to a downstream component.

151.name: Improper Neutralization of Comment Delimiters
151.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as comment delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

152.name: Improper Neutralization of Macro Symbols
152.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as macro symbols when they are sent to a downstream component.

153.name: Improper Neutralization of Substitution Characters
153.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as substitution characters when they are sent to a downstream component.

154.name: Improper Neutralization of Variable Name Delimiters
154.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as variable name delimiters when they are sent to a downstream component.

155.name: Improper Neutralization of Wildcards or Matching Symbols
155.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as wildcards or matching symbols when they are sent to a downstream component.

156.name: Improper Neutralization of Whitespace
156.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could be interpreted as whitespace when they are sent to a downstream component.

157.name: Failure to Sanitize Paired Delimiters
157.summary: The product does not properly handle the characters that are used to mark the beginning and ending of a group of entities, such as parentheses, brackets, and braces.

158.name: Improper Neutralization of Null Byte or NUL Character
158.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes NUL characters or null bytes when they are sent to a downstream component.

159.name: Improper Handling of Invalid Use of Special Elements
159.summary: The product does not properly filter, remove, quote, or otherwise manage the invalid use of special elements in user-controlled input, which could cause adverse effect on its behavior and integrity.

160.name: Improper Neutralization of Leading Special Elements
160.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes leading special elements that could be interpreted in unexpected ways when they are sent to a downstream component.

161.name: Improper Neutralization of Multiple Leading Special Elements
161.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes multiple leading special elements that could be interpreted in unexpected ways when they are sent to a downstream component.

162.name: Improper Neutralization of Trailing Special Elements
162.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes trailing special elements that could be interpreted in unexpected ways when they are sent to a downstream component.

163.name: Improper Neutralization of Multiple Trailing Special Elements
163.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes multiple trailing special elements that could be interpreted in unexpected ways when they are sent to a downstream component.

164.name: Improper Neutralization of Internal Special Elements
164.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes internal special elements that could be interpreted in unexpected ways when they are sent to a downstream component.

165.name: Improper Neutralization of Multiple Internal Special Elements
165.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes multiple internal special elements that could be interpreted in unexpected ways when they are sent to a downstream component.

166.name: Improper Handling of Missing Special Element
166.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not handle or incorrectly handles when an expected special element is missing.

167.name: Improper Handling of Additional Special Element
167.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not handle or incorrectly handles when an additional unexpected special element is provided.

168.name: Improper Handling of Inconsistent Special Elements
168.summary: The product does not properly handle input in which an inconsistency exists between two or more special characters or reserved words.

170.name: Improper Null Termination
170.summary: The product does not terminate or incorrectly terminates a string or array with a null character or equivalent terminator.

Should the null character corrupt the process flow, or affect a flag controlling access, it may lead to logical errors which allow for the execution of arbitrary code.

172.name: Encoding Error
172.summary: The product does not properly encode or decode the data, resulting in unexpected values.

173.name: Improper Handling of Alternate Encoding
173.summary: The product does not properly handle when an input uses an alternate encoding that is valid for the control sphere to which the input is being sent.

174.name: Double Decoding of the Same Data
174.summary: The product decodes the same input twice, which can limit the effectiveness of any protection mechanism that occurs in between the decoding operations.

175.name: Improper Handling of Mixed Encoding
175.summary: The product does not properly handle when the same input uses several different (mixed) encodings.

176.name: Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding
176.summary: The product does not properly handle when an input contains Unicode encoding.

177.name: Improper Handling of URL Encoding (Hex Encoding)
177.summary: The product does not properly handle when all or part of an input has been URL encoded.

178.name: Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity
178.summary: The product does not properly account for differences in case sensitivity when accessing or determining the properties of a resource, leading to inconsistent results.

179.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Early Validation
179.summary: The product validates input before applying protection mechanisms that modify the input, which could allow an attacker to bypass the validation via dangerous inputs that only arise after the modification.

consequences.note: An attacker could include dangerous input that bypasses validation protection mechanisms which can be used to launch various attacks including injection attacks, execute arbitrary code or cause other unintended behavior.

180.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Canonicalize
180.summary: The product validates input before it is canonicalized, which prevents the product from detecting data that becomes invalid after the canonicalization step.

181.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Filter
181.summary: The product validates data before it has been filtered, which prevents the product from detecting data that becomes invalid after the filtering step.

182.name: Collapse of Data into Unsafe Value
182.summary: The product filters data in a way that causes it to be reduced or "collapsed" into an unsafe value that violates an expected security property.

183.name: Permissive List of Allowed Inputs
183.summary: The product implements a protection mechanism that relies on a list of inputs (or properties of inputs) that are explicitly allowed by policy because the inputs are assumed to be safe, but the list is too permissive - that is, it allows an input that is unsafe, leading to resultant weaknesses.

184.name: Incomplete List of Disallowed Inputs
184.summary: The product implements a protection mechanism that relies on a list of inputs (or properties of inputs) that are not allowed by policy or otherwise require other action to neutralize before additional processing takes place, but the list is incomplete, leading to resultant weaknesses.

185.name: Incorrect Regular Expression
185.summary: The product specifies a regular expression in a way that causes data to be improperly matched or compared.

consequences.note: When the regular expression is not correctly specified, data might have a different format or type than the rest of the program expects, producing resultant weaknesses or errors.
In PHP, regular expression checks can sometimes be bypassed with a null byte, leading to any number of weaknesses.

186.name: Overly Restrictive Regular Expression
186.summary: A regular expression is overly restrictive, which prevents dangerous values from being detected.

187.name: Partial String Comparison
187.summary: The product performs a comparison that only examines a portion of a factor before determining whether there is a match, such as a substring, leading to resultant weaknesses.

188.name: Reliance on Data/Memory Layout
188.summary: The product makes invalid assumptions about how protocol data or memory is organized at a lower level, resulting in unintended program behavior.

consequences.note: Can result in unintended modifications or exposure of sensitive memory.

190.name: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
190.summary: The product performs a calculation that can produce an integer overflow or wraparound when the logic assumes that the resulting value will always be larger than the original value. This occurs when an integer value is incremented to a value that is too large to store in the associated representation. When this occurs, the value may become a very small or negative number.

191.summary: The product subtracts one value from another, such that the result is less than the minimum allowable integer value, which produces a value that is not equal to the correct result.

consequences.note: This weakness will generally lead to undefined behavior and therefore crashes. In the case of overflows involving loop index variables, the likelihood of infinite loops is also high.

This weakness can sometimes trigger buffer overflows which can be used to execute arbitrary code. This is usually outside the scope of a program's implicit security policy.

192.name: Integer Coercion Error
192.summary: Integer coercion refers to a set of flaws pertaining to the type casting, extension, or truncation of primitive data types.

consequences.note: Integer coercion often leads to undefined states of execution resulting in infinite loops or crashes.
In some cases, integer coercion errors can lead to exploitable buffer overflow conditions, resulting in the execution of arbitrary code.
Integer coercion errors result in an incorrect value being stored for the variable in question.

193.name: Off-by-one Error
193.summary: A product calculates or uses an incorrect maximum or minimum value that is 1 more, or 1 less, than the correct value.

consequences.note: This weakness will generally lead to undefined behavior and therefore crashes. In the case of overflows involving loop index variables, the likelihood of infinite loops is also high.

If the value in question is important to data (as opposed to flow), simple data corruption has occurred. Also, if the wrap around results in other conditions such as buffer overflows, further memory corruption may occur.
This weakness can sometimes trigger buffer overflows which can be used to execute arbitrary code. This is usually outside the scope of a program's implicit security policy.

194.name: Unexpected Sign Extension
194.summary: The product performs an operation on a number that causes it to be sign extended when it is transformed into a larger data type. When the original number is negative, this can produce unexpected values that lead to resultant weaknesses.

195.name: Signed to Unsigned Conversion Error
195.summary: The product uses a signed primitive and performs a cast to an unsigned primitive, which can produce an unexpected value if the value of the signed primitive can not be represented using an unsigned primitive.

consequences.note: Conversion between signed and unsigned values can lead to a variety of errors, but from a security standpoint is most commonly associated with integer overflow and buffer overflow vulnerabilities.

196.name: Unsigned to Signed Conversion Error
196.summary: The product uses an unsigned primitive and performs a cast to a signed primitive, which can produce an unexpected value if the value of the unsigned primitive can not be represented using a signed primitive.

consequences.note: Incorrect sign conversions generally lead to undefined behavior, and therefore crashes.
If a poor cast lead to a buffer overflow or similar condition, data integrity may be affected.

197.name: Numeric Truncation Error
197.summary: Truncation errors occur when a primitive is cast to a primitive of a smaller size and data is lost in the conversion.

consequences.note: The true value of the data is lost and corrupted data is used.

198.name: Use of Incorrect Byte Ordering
198.summary: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not account for byte ordering (e.g. big-endian and little-endian) when processing the input, causing an incorrect number or value to be used.

20.name: Improper Input Validation
20.summary: The product receives input or data, but it does not validate or incorrectly validates that the input has the properties that are required to process the data safely and correctly.

consequences.note: An attacker could provide unexpected values and cause a program crash or excessive consumption of resources, such as memory and CPU.
An attacker could read confidential data if they are able to control resource references.
An attacker could use malicious input to modify data or possibly alter control flow in unexpected ways, including arbitrary command execution.

200.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
200.summary: The product exposes sensitive information to an actor that is not explicitly authorized to have access to that information.

201.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data
201.summary: The code transmits data to another actor, but a portion of the data includes sensitive information that should not be accessible to that actor.

consequences.note: Sensitive data may be exposed to attackers.

202.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information Through Data Queries
202.summary: When trying to keep information confidential, an attacker can often infer some of the information by using statistics.

consequences.note: Sensitive information may possibly be leaked through data queries accidentally.

203.summary: The product behaves differently or sends different responses under different circumstances in a way that is observable to an unauthorized actor, which exposes security-relevant information about the state of the product, such as whether a particular operation was successful or not.

consequences.note: An attacker can gain access to sensitive information about the system, including authentication information that may allow an attacker to gain access to the system.

206.name: Observable Internal Behavioral Discrepancy
206.summary: The product performs multiple behaviors that are combined to produce a single result, but the individual behaviors are observable separately in a way that allows attackers to reveal internal state or internal decision points.

207.name: Observable Behavioral Discrepancy With Equivalent Products
207.summary: The product operates in an environment in which its existence or specific identity should not be known, but it behaves differently than other products with equivalent functionality, in a way that is observable to an attacker.

208.name: Observable Timing Discrepancy
208.summary: Two separate operations in a product require different amounts of time to complete, in a way that is observable to an actor and reveals security-relevant information about the state of the product, such as whether a particular operation was successful or not.

209.name: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
209.summary: The product generates an error message that includes sensitive information about its environment, users, or associated data.

consequences.note: Often this will either reveal sensitive information which may be used for a later attack or private information stored in the server.

210.name: Self-generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
210.summary: The product identifies an error condition and creates its own diagnostic or error messages that contain sensitive information.

211.name: Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
211.summary: The product performs an operation that triggers an external diagnostic or error message that is not directly generated or controlled by the product, such as an error generated by the programming language interpreter that a software application uses. The error can contain sensitive system information.

212.name: Improper Removal of Sensitive Information Before Storage or Transfer
212.summary: The product stores, transfers, or shares a resource that contains sensitive information, but it does not properly remove that information before the product makes the resource available to unauthorized actors.

213.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information Due to Incompatible Policies
213.summary: The product's intended functionality exposes information to certain actors in accordance with the developer's security policy, but this information is regarded as sensitive according to the intended security policies of other stakeholders such as the product's administrator, users, or others whose information is being processed.

214.name: Invocation of Process Using Visible Sensitive Information
214.summary: A process is invoked with sensitive command-line arguments, environment variables, or other elements that can be seen by other processes on the operating system.

215.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Debugging Code
215.summary: The product inserts sensitive information into debugging code, which could expose this information if the debugging code is not disabled in production.

219.name: Storage of File with Sensitive Data Under Web Root
219.summary: The product stores sensitive data under the web document root with insufficient access control, which might make it accessible to untrusted parties.

22.summary: The product uses external input to construct a pathname that is intended to identify a file or directory that is located underneath a restricted parent directory, but the product does not properly neutralize special elements within the pathname that can cause the pathname to resolve to a location that is outside of the restricted directory.

220.name: Storage of File With Sensitive Data Under FTP Root
220.summary: The product stores sensitive data under the FTP server root with insufficient access control, which might make it accessible to untrusted parties.

221.name: Information Loss or Omission
221.summary: The product does not record, or improperly records, security-relevant information that leads to an incorrect decision or hampers later analysis.

222.name: Truncation of Security-relevant Information
222.summary: The product truncates the display, recording, or processing of security-relevant information in a way that can obscure the source or nature of an attack.

consequences.note: The source of an attack will be difficult or impossible to determine. This can allow attacks to the system to continue without notice.

223.name: Omission of Security-relevant Information
223.summary: The product does not record or display information that would be important for identifying the source or nature of an attack, or determining if an action is safe.

consequences.note: The source of an attack will be difficult or impossible to determine. This can allow attacks to the system to continue without notice.

224.name: Obscured Security-relevant Information by Alternate Name
224.summary: The product records security-relevant information according to an alternate name of the affected entity, instead of the canonical name.

225.name: DEPRECATED: General Information Management Problems
225.summary: This weakness can be found at CWE-199.

226.name: Sensitive Information in Resource Not Removed Before Reuse
226.summary: The product releases a resource such as memory or a file so that it can be made available for reuse, but it does not clear or "zeroize" the information contained in the resource before the product performs a critical state transition or makes the resource available for reuse by other entities.

228.name: Improper Handling of Syntactically Invalid Structure
228.summary: The product does not handle or incorrectly handles input that is not syntactically well-formed with respect to the associated specification.

consequences.note: If an input is syntactically invalid, then processing the input could place the system in an unexpected state that could lead to a crash, consume available system resources or other unintended behaviors.

229.name: Improper Handling of Values
229.summary: The product does not properly handle when the expected number of values for parameters, fields, or arguments is not provided in input, or if those values are undefined.

23.name: Relative Path Traversal
23.summary: The product uses external input to construct a pathname that should be within a restricted directory, but it does not properly neutralize sequences such as ".." that can resolve to a location that is outside of that directory.

consequences.note: The attacker may be able to create or overwrite critical files that are used to execute code, such as programs or libraries.
